title: Evaluating a Model Without Fooling Yourself
subtitle: Overfitting, out-of-sample testing, walk-forward validation, and drift — the difference between a model that looks good and one that actually works.
attribution: Original explanations written for this app. Standard machine-learning evaluation concepts (train/test split, cross-validation, walk-forward, distribution drift) in plain language for someone operating an automated trading system.
audience: the operator of an automated ICT trading bot that has an ML lifecycle — shadow models, a candidate→shadow→advisory promotion ladder, and KS/PSI drift monitoring. Tie every concept to backtest-vs-live, to shadow-testing a model before it's allowed to influence a real order, and to why a great backtest can still lose money live. Keep the ML evaluation concepts front and centre; the trading system is the running example, not the subject.

episodes.title: Overfitting — when a model memorises the past
episodes.focus: What a model actually is (a learned mapping from input features to a target/label). Overfitting: fitting the NOISE instead of the signal — memorising the training examples rather than learning the pattern, so it scores beautifully on data it has seen and poorly on anything new. The train / validation / test split and the cardinal rule: never judge a model on data it trained on. The bias–variance intuition — too simple underfits (misses the pattern), too complex overfits (chases noise); the sweet spot generalises. The direct trading analogy: a strategy whose parameters are tuned until they perfectly fit historical trades is a CURVE-FIT — the same failure as an overfit model, and it's why an amazing backtest is a warning sign, not a green light.

episodes.title: Out-of-sample & walk-forward — testing on the future
episodes.focus: In-sample vs out-of-sample: the only honest test is on data the model has never seen. The holdout set. k-fold cross-validation for ordinary data — and why you CANNOT shuffle or k-fold time-series data: doing so leaks the future into the past (look-ahead bias / data leakage), producing a fantasy score. Walk-forward (rolling-window) validation: train on a window, test on the NEXT unseen window, roll forward, repeat — the honest way to evaluate a time-series model or a trading strategy. Concrete leakage traps: normalising features using whole-history statistics, labels that peek at future bars, tuning on the test set. The takeaway: an out-of-sample / walk-forward result is worth ten in-sample ones.

episodes.title: It worked, then it didn't — drift, regime change & honest live evaluation
episodes.focus: Why a validated model still decays live. Distribution drift: the live data stops looking like the training data — and why you measure it with tests like KS (does the score distribution still match?) and PSI (population stability index). Regime change in markets as the canonical cause — a model trained in a trending market fails when the market goes choppy. The gap between offline metrics (accuracy, AUC) and the only metric that pays: live outcome / PnL. Shadow-testing as the fix — run the model live but don't let it act, log its predictions, and compare to reality BEFORE it's promoted to influence real orders; this is exactly what a candidate → shadow → advisory ladder does. The closing discipline: never trust a single number, always evaluate on the future, and keep watching for drift after deployment.

sources:
Teach how to evaluate a machine-learning model (or a trading strategy) honestly — expand these concept notes into original, plain-language explanations; do not copy any text.

SECTION A — What a model is, and overfitting.
- A supervised model learns a mapping from INPUT FEATURES (e.g. recent volatility, trend strength, time-of-day) to a TARGET/LABEL (e.g. 'did this setup win?'). 'Training' = adjusting the model so its predictions match the labelled examples.
- OVERFITTING is the central danger: a model flexible enough can MEMORISE the training examples — fitting the random noise, not the underlying pattern. It then scores near-perfect on the data it saw and falls apart on anything new. The model didn't learn; it memorised.
- TRAIN / VALIDATION / TEST split: hold data aside. Train on the training set; tune choices on the validation set; measure final honest performance on a test set the model has NEVER seen and you only look at once. Cardinal rule: NEVER evaluate on data the model trained on — that number is meaningless (it measures memory, not generalisation).
- BIAS–VARIANCE intuition: too-simple model = high bias = underfits (misses the real pattern); too-complex model = high variance = overfits (chases noise). Good generalisation is the balance. More complexity is not more skill.
- TRADING ANALOGY (the throughline): a strategy whose parameters are tuned until they fit historical trades perfectly is a CURVE-FIT — mathematically the same failure as an overfit model. That's why a spectacular backtest should INCREASE your suspicion, not your confidence: the more you optimised on the past, the more you probably fit its noise.

SECTION B — Out-of-sample and walk-forward validation.
- IN-SAMPLE = data used to build/tune the model. OUT-OF-SAMPLE = data withheld and untouched until the final test. Only out-of-sample performance predicts the future.
- HOLDOUT: set aside a chunk (say the last 20%) and never train on it. K-FOLD CROSS-VALIDATION: rotate which fold is the test set to use data efficiently — fine for INDEPENDENT data.
- TIME-SERIES CAVEAT (critical): you cannot shuffle or randomly k-fold time-ordered data. Random splits let the model train on FUTURE bars and test on PAST ones — LOOK-AHEAD BIAS / DATA LEAKAGE — which inflates the score into a fantasy. Time must only ever flow forward in evaluation.
- WALK-FORWARD (rolling-window) VALIDATION: train on a window of history, test on the NEXT chunk the model has not seen, record the result, roll the window forward, repeat. Averaging those out-of-sample chunks is the honest estimate of live performance — for both ML models and trading strategies.
- LEAKAGE TRAPS to name concretely: normalising/scaling features using statistics computed over the WHOLE dataset (peeks at the future); labels built from information not available at decision time; selecting features or tuning hyper-parameters on the test set; survivorship bias in the data. Any of these turns a bad model into a great-looking one.

SECTION C — Drift, regime change, and honest live evaluation.
- Even a properly validated model DECAYS in production because the world changes. DISTRIBUTION DRIFT: the statistical distribution of live inputs (or of the model's output scores) stops matching what it was trained on.
- Measuring drift: the KOLMOGOROV–SMIRNOV (KS) test asks 'is the current score distribution still the same as the reference one?'; the POPULATION STABILITY INDEX (PSI) buckets the distributions and sums how far they've moved. A rising KS/PSI is an early warning that the model is operating outside its training conditions.
- REGIME CHANGE is the canonical market cause: a model (or strategy) trained mostly on trending markets can fail badly when volatility regime flips to choppy/range-bound. The pattern it learned no longer holds.
- The OFFLINE-vs-LIVE GAP: good offline metrics (accuracy, AUC, precision/recall) do NOT guarantee live profit — costs, slippage, latency, and drift all bite. The only metric that ultimately matters is realised outcome / PnL on live, unseen data.
- SHADOW-TESTING (the fix): deploy the model LIVE but in observe-only mode — it makes predictions and you log them, but it is not allowed to change any real decision. You then compare its live predictions to what actually happened, accumulating an honest out-of-sample track record, BEFORE promoting it to influence real orders. A staged ladder — candidate (research only) → shadow (logs live, no influence) → advisory (allowed to influence) — is exactly this discipline made into a process; promotion past shadow is the real go-live gate.
- CLOSING DISCIPLINE: never trust a single number; always evaluate on data from the FUTURE relative to training; prefer walk-forward to a single split; and keep monitoring for drift AFTER deployment, because 'it validated once' is not 'it works forever'.
